c.v: In a few sentences and without notes, explain why ROS messages and tf2 store a 3D orientation as a quaternion instead of as roll, pitch and yaw. Name two problems with Euler angles, and what the quaternion costs you in return. Take 10 minutes.

Three angles mean nothing until you fix a convention: which axes, in which order, and whether the axes stay fixed or move with the body. REP 103 counts 24 valid conventions. Even with the convention fixed, the angles have a singularity. At a pitch of ±90° the roll axis and the yaw axis line up, one degree of freedom disappears, which is called

, and near that pose a turn of one degree can change the roll and yaw readings by 180°. Angles also don't compose or interpolate by adding them: yaw 170° and yaw −170° are 20° apart, and their average, 0°, points the opposite way.

A unit quaternion (x, y, z, w) covers every rotation without a singularity. Two rotations compose with one quaternion product of 16 multiplications, and slerp interpolates between two orientations along the shortest arc at a constant rate. The price is one redundant number. The four components must keep a norm of 1, rounding makes the norm drift, and code has to normalise. Every rotation also has two quaternions, q and −q, so comparing or averaging them needs care. A rotation matrix has no singularity either, but it stores nine numbers held together by six constraints.

You pass if you named the convention problem or gimbal lock, the trouble with composing or interpolating angles, and the unit-norm constraint. One problem and no cost is a partial pass. "Quaternions are faster" on its own is a fail.

An orientation in 3D can be written three ways. Roll, pitch and yaw are three angles about three axes, in a fixed order agreed on before the numbers mean anything. A rotation matrix turns coordinates directly, with no such ambiguity. A unit quaternion stores the same rotation as four numbers, an axis and a half-angle folded together, written as x, y, z, then w.

The problem is that three angles alone don't determine a rotation: the same numbers mean a different orientation depending on which axes are used, in which order, and whether they are fixed to the world or the body, and many conventions are valid at once. Even with a convention fixed, angles carry a singularity: at one orientation two of the three axes line up, one degree of freedom disappears, and a tiny turn there can swing two readings by a huge amount, the failure called gimbal lock. Angles also don't average correctly by adding the numbers, because the numbers wrap where the rotations don't.

A unit quaternion sidesteps both problems: it represents every orientation with no singularity, two quaternions compose by one multiplication in a fixed formula, and interpolating along the shortest path is a closed formula too, something roll, pitch and yaw cannot do correctly. A rotation matrix shares the no-singularity property but spends nine numbers on three degrees of freedom, tied by constraints that rounding slowly loosens.

The quaternion's own cost is a fourth, redundant number: it must stay unit length or the rotation is subtly wrong, so code composing many of them has to renormalise now and then. Every rotation also has two quaternions representing it, a number and its exact negative, so comparing orientations by their four numbers directly is wrong; you compare how close their product is to no rotation instead. Roll, pitch and yaw remain right for reading a number aloud or plotting one over time, and gimbal lock matters only to a body that can reach that orientation, ruling it out for a wheeled robot but not an arm or drone.

This is the interview question itself: naming the convention problem and gimbal lock as what roll, pitch and yaw cost, and the extra number with the double meaning of a sign as what a quaternion costs back, which is why ROS and tf2 store orientation as a quaternion and convert to angles only for a person to read.
Turn the nose of a robot, which starts on the x axis, by 90° about z and by 90° about y, once in each order:

Yaw first turns the nose to the left, along y, and the pitch about y then leaves it there. Pitch first points the nose at the floor, and a yaw about the vertical axis can't move a vector that lies on that axis. Rotations in 3D don't commute, so three angles describe an orientation only together with an order and a choice of axes.

. Its columns are where the x, y and z axes end up, so the columns are orthonormal and the determinant is +1. The inverse is the transpose, and "apply B, then A" is the product A·B, read from right to left. A rotation matrix composes and inverts cleanly, but it spends nine numbers on three degrees of freedom, and the six constraints between them are what rounding slowly breaks.

REP 103 fixes the convention for ROS. Roll, pitch and yaw are rotations about the fixed x, y and z axes, applied in that order, so R = Rz(yaw)·Ry(pitch)·Rx(roll). Read from the robot's point of view, the same matrix is a yaw about the robot's own z axis, then a pitch about its new y axis, then a roll about its newest x axis. Both readings produce the same matrix, which is why you meet both descriptions. REP 103 lists quaternions as the preferred representation, then rotation matrices, then these fixed-axis angles, and it discourages other Euler angle conventions because 24 of them are valid and different fields default to different ones.

The camera from the topic on poses is an example. Its URDF gives the optical frame a roll of −1.57 and a yaw of −1.57, which stand for −90°. Rz(−90°)·Rx(−90°) has the columns (0, −1, 0), (0, 0, −1) and (1, 0, 0), exactly the matrix
that the worked example there wrote down column by column: image right is the camera's −y, image down is its −z, and the viewing direction is its +x.
stores a rotation by the angle θ about the unit axis n as four numbers: x, y and z are n·sin(θ/2), and w is cos(θ/2). ROS writes them in that order, with w last. The message
fields that default to (0, 0, 0, 1), the rotation that does nothing. Eigen's
constructor takes w first. Mixing the two orders is a classic bug, and the code below names every field with a designated initialiser so that the order can't be misread.
Here are the operations in plain C++: the product that composes two rotations, the sandwich q·v·q* that rotates a vector, and slerp:

blocks.text:
yaw 90:      (x 0.000, y 0.000, z 0.707, w 0.707) turns the nose to (0.000, 1.000, 0.000)
its negative (x 0.000, y 0.000, z -0.707, w -0.707) turns the nose to (0.000, 1.000, 0.000)
halfway from 170 to -170: average of angles 0.0, slerp 180.0

You can't compare orientations by comparing components, because a filter or a library may hand you either sign; compare |q1·q2| with 1 instead. And interpolation has to pick a sign first.
That is what the last line shows. The average of the angles, 0°, points backwards, because the numbers wrap at ±180° and the orientations don't.

The product of two unit quaternions has norm 1 in exact arithmetic. In floating point it drifts, so code that composes many small rotations divides by the norm now and then. A normalised quaternion has three degrees of freedom, like the rotation it stands for.

subs.title: Probability basics and covariance in pose messages

c.v: Echo the odometry of the bench robot, with the simulation from the robot world project running, and look at the uncertainty field:
It prints a list of 36 zeros. The Gazebo DiffDrive system publishes
, which has no covariance, and the bridge's conversion to

leaves the field at its default. A zero variance claims that the pose is known exactly. Any consumer that fuses this odometry needs a covariance from somewhere else, and to supply one you need the few ideas below.
A measured quantity such as the robot's x position is a
: repeat the same drive, and it comes out a little different each time. Its
μ is the average over many repetitions. Its
σ² is the average squared distance from the mean, and its
σ is the square root of the variance, in the same unit as the quantity. For x in metres, the variance is in m² and σ is in metres. Many errors are close to
, the bell curve, and for a Gaussian in one dimension 68 % of the values fall within 1σ of the mean, 95 % within 2σ and 99.7 % within 3σ.
Two quantities can vary together. Their

is the average of (x − μx)(y − μy): positive when x tends to be large when y is large, negative when the opposite holds, and zero when neither tells you anything about the other. Divided by σx·σy it becomes the
, a number from −1 to 1. For n quantities the variances and covariances form an n × n
. The variances are on the diagonal, the matrix is symmetric because cov(x, y) = cov(y, x), and it is positive semi-definite: no combination of the quantities has a negative variance.

, stored row by row. The rows and columns are x, y, z, then rotation about the fixed x, y and z axes, so the yaw variance is at index 35 and the x-y covariance appears twice, at indices 1 and 6. The units are m² in the top-left block, rad² in the bottom-right block, and m·rad between them.
has one such matrix for the pose and one for the twist.
uses three 3 × 3 matrices, and its message definition gives two conventions: all zeros means the covariance is unknown, and −1 in element 0 means the sensor gives no estimate of that quantity at all.
Here is how to read such a matrix, for an odometry estimate with σx = 0.2 m, σy = 0.1 m, an x-y covariance of 0.012 m² and σyaw = 0.05 rad:

blocks.text:
x-y at indices 1 and 6, yaw variance at index 35
sigma x 0.200 m, sigma y 0.100 m, sigma yaw 0.050 rad (2.86 deg)
correlation of x and y: 0.60
inside the 1-sigma ellipse: 39.3 %
95 % ellipse: 0.515 m by 0.186 m, long axis at 19.3 deg
sideways sigma after    1 m straight: 0.050 m
sideways sigma after   10 m straight: 0.500 m
sideways sigma after   50 m straight: 2.500 m

c.v: The diagonal gives the σ values directly, after a square root. The positive correlation of 0.6 tilts the uncertainty: the points of equal probability form an ellipse whose long axis lies 19.3° from x, along the eigenvector of the 2 × 2 block, with the square roots of the eigenvalues as its semi-axes at 1σ. RViz's Odometry display draws this ellipse through its Covariance option.

The fourth line breaks a common assumption. The 68 % rule is for one dimension. In two dimensions only 39.3 % of a Gaussian lies inside the 1σ ellipse, and a 95 % ellipse needs 2.448σ, because the share inside k standard deviations is 1 − e^(−k²/2). If a requirement says "within 0.5 m with 95 % confidence", compare 0.5 m with the 95 % ellipse, not with σ.

The last three lines show why odometry uncertainty grows without limit. A heading that is off by a fixed small angle δ moves the robot sideways by about d·δ after d metres, so a yaw σ of 0.05 rad becomes a sideways σ of 0.5 m after 10 m and 2.5 m after 50 m. Over longer drives the cloud of possible positions bends into a curved band, because a heading error carries the robot along an arc. This growth is why odometry alone drifts and why REP 105 separates the smooth
frame. The topic on frames with tf2 builds on this.

Gimbal lock does more than remove a degree of freedom at exactly 90°. Every angle triple near it is badly conditioned, and the readout jumps as the body passes through. Tilt a body about y from 88° to 92°, as the tool of a robot arm does when it turns past vertical, and convert each orientation to roll, pitch and yaw. The second half of the program shows what averaging quaternions component by component does:

blocks.text:
tilting about y past vertical:
  88 deg: y 0.695, w 0.719 -> roll 0.0, pitch 88.0, yaw 0.0
  89 deg: y 0.701, w 0.713 -> roll 0.0, pitch 89.0, yaw 0.0
  90 deg: y 0.707, w 0.707 -> roll 0.0, pitch 90.0, yaw 0.0
  91 deg: y 0.713, w 0.701 -> roll 180.0, pitch 89.0, yaw 180.0
  92 deg: y 0.719, w 0.695 -> roll 180.0, pitch 88.0, yaw 180.0
mean of yaw 90 and yaw 0: norm 0.924, squared 0.854
  normalized: yaw 45.0
mean of q and -q: norm 0.000, normalized has a value: false

c.v: The quaternion changes by about 0.006 per degree, all the way through. The angles are continuous until 90°, then roll and yaw jump by 180° while the pitch turns around, because a pitch beyond 90° is written as a pitch below 90° with the body flipped over. Both triples are correct. A controller that works on the angle difference, or a plot of the log, sees a jump that the body never made. Keep orientations as quaternions or matrices in code, compute errors with quaternion products, and convert to angles only for display, or for a robot that stays far from ±90° pitch, such as a wheeled base where the yaw alone is safe.
Where does an unnormalised quaternion come from? Rarely from drift in
. Composing 3.6 million products of one small rotation, an hour of a 1 kHz gyro, kept the norm within 1.6e-10 of 1 in
with GCC 13. The same loop in

moves it by whole per cent, and the direction depends on the step: about the unit axis (0.48, 0.6, 0.64), steps of 0.001 rad grew the norm by 3.1 %, steps of 0.01 rad shrank it by 5.9 %, and steps of 0.0005 rad shrank it by 16.7 %. The common sources are hand-typed values such as (0, 0, 0.7, 0.7), values rounded to a few decimals in a YAML file or a launch argument, and averages taken component by component. The mean of yaw 0° and yaw 90° has a norm of 0.924 and a squared norm of 0.854. After normalising, it is the correct 45°, but only after. Worse, when one of two readings of the same heading arrives as −q, which a filter or a driver is free to send, the component mean is the zero quaternion. It has no direction at all, and no normalisation rescues it. To average orientations, flip each quaternion so its dot product with the first is positive, then average, then normalise.
tf2 refuses an unnormalised rotation instead of guessing.
